summary: Provides guidelines for implementing and using IPFIX, including template management, transport-specific issues, exporting and collecting processes, and use on middleboxes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a helpful how-to for people building traffic-reporting tools, with tips on avoiding common problems.

subtitle: Practical advice for building IPFIX exporters and collectors, from Templates to transports to middleboxes.

tldr.problem: The IPFIX protocol leaves many practical choices open, and early implementations made mistakes that caused interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives guidelines on Template management, exporting and collecting, SCTP, UDP and TCP transport, middleboxes, TLS and DTLS security, extending the information model, and a list of common mistakes.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get concrete defaults and warnings, but the normative rules stay in RFC 5101 and RFC 5102. This document is Informational and defines no protocol.

sections.title: What the Guidelines Cover
sections.content:
The IPFIX protocol (RFC 5101) defines how IP Flow information is exported from routers, measurement probes and other devices. In IPFIX, a Template lists { type, length } pairs that say which fields appear in the Data Records that follow. Templates are sent rarely compared with Data Records, which saves bandwidth. The standard Information Elements come from the information model (RFC 5102).

This RFC groups its advice into seven sets: Template management, Exporting Process, Collecting Process, transport, middleboxes, security, and extending the information model. It ends with common mistakes. It does not use RFC 2119 key words except when quoting the IPFIX standards, and the normative text remains in RFC 5101 and RFC 5102.
sections.eli5: A tool that reports network traffic sends a form layout once, then many filled-in forms. This guide helps people build such tools without common slip-ups.

sections.title: Templates, Exporting and Collecting
sections.content:
The Exporting Process should always try to send Template Records before the Data Records that use them. A Collecting Process may hold Data Records with an unknown Template ID for a while. If no Template arrives, the RFC recommends logging and discarding them, and resetting the Transport Session for SCTP and TCP. The wait should be configurable, with a recommended default of 30 minutes.

Template IDs are managed by the Exporter and are unique per Transport Session and Observation Domain. If IDs run short, the Exporter sends a Template Withdrawal Message (not possible over UDP). A restart of the session may renumber Template IDs. Options Templates add scope, trading simplicity for bandwidth efficiency. The root scope of every message is the Observation Domain.

Other guidance:

  • Set IDs 0 and 1 are unused, 2 is a Template Set, 3 an Options Template Set, 4 to 255 are reserved and higher values are Data Sets.
  • Delta counters tolerate loss better than Total counters.
  • Alignment can be done with the paddingOctets Information Element.
  • Clocks should be synchronized to a UTC source, and timestamp precision should not exceed what the Metering Process has.
  • A Collector should store data at full size even if Templates use reduced-size encoding, and should handle unknown Information Elements as octet arrays or ignore them.
sections.eli5: First you send the blank form layout, then the filled-in forms. If forms arrive without their layout, the receiver waits a while and then gives up.

sections.title: Choosing SCTP, UDP or TCP
sections.content:
IPFIX implementations MUST support SCTP with partial reliability extensions (PR-SCTP) and MAY support TCP and UDP. The RFC calls PR-SCTP the preferred transport because it is congestion-aware and has a simpler state machine than TCP. It offers multiple streams, which avoid head-of-line blocking, and per-message reliability. Billing or security data can be sent reliably while capacity planning can tolerate loss. Template Sets and Withdrawals must not use partial reliability, and unordered delivery should not be used for Templates or Total counters. Stream configuration has to be done out of band.

UDP is not recommended. It suits only dedicated, managed networks in a single administrative domain where SCTP is unavailable and the Collector is close to the Exporter, such as replacing an existing NetFlow setup. The RFC says export traffic in such cases amounts to 2-5% of the monitored interface's bandwidth. Over UDP, Templates MUST be resent at configurable intervals. Recommended defaults are every 10 minutes (configurable from 1 minute to 1 day) and every 20 packets (configurable from 1 to 1000). The Collector should expire Templates after three times the refresh rate, or 60 minutes if nothing is configured. Message sizes are bound by the path MTU, or 512 bytes if it is unknown.

TCP fits when SCTP is unavailable but reliable delivery is needed, or the network is not provisioned for IPFIX traffic. Exporters need not resend Templates. If bandwidth is short, TCP congestion control may make the Exporter block.
sections.eli5: SCTP is like a delivery service where you pick how careful each parcel is handled. UDP is a postcard with no guarantee, and TCP is registered mail that can pile up if the roads are jammed.

sections.title: Middleboxes and NetFlow v9 Pitfalls
sections.content:
Middleboxes such as NATs, firewalls, tunnel endpoints and packet markers change or drop packets, so one flow entering is not the same flow leaving. The RFC recommends putting the Observation Point on a boundary between middlebox functions, not inside one, and clearly telling Collectors where it is. It also recommends being able to report packets dropped per Flow, both the observed and the post-change DSCP value, and the translated IP addresses and port numbers. When values vary within a flow, the first observed value is reported.

The common mistakes section lists differences from NetFlow version 9 (RFC 3954): IPFIX needs a congestion-aware transport and uses version number 10 where NetFlow uses 9. The IPFIX header length field is the total message length in octets, not a record count. Options Template scope must not be empty, and Set IDs 0 and 1 are not used. Padding must be shorter than the shortest record, or it is read as another record. Information Element numbers run from 0 to 32767, and setting the high bit marks an enterprise-specific element.
sections.eli5: If a box in the middle changes the address on your parcel, the report must say whether you counted before or after the change. And do not mix up the new form with an older, similar-looking one.

sections.title: Security and Extending the Model
sections.content:
TLS (over TCP) and DTLS (over UDP, SCTP and PR-SCTP) are the required ways to secure IPFIX. The Exporter acts as the TLS client and the Collector as the server. Both sides must use strong mutual authentication with X.509 certificates, and verify the peer against a set of authorized peers and its fully-qualified domain name. TLS over TCP was the most mature option at the time, so the RFC recommended it for secure transport. DTLS implementations were still under development, and the RFC warned of vulnerabilities in DTLS over SCTP and advised caution in production.

Reporting middlebox internals is itself sensitive: dropped-packet counts can help attackers study a firewall, and reported translations can reveal hidden network structure or weaken an anonymizer, so this data must be protected.

New Information Elements of general interest go into the IANA registry after expert review. Enterprises can define their own with identifiers in the range 1-32767 coupled with a Private Enterprise Number registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: Both sides must show ID cards before swapping reports, because the reports can reveal how a network is built.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Reserved for future use; a Collector ignores them.

items.label: Data Set
items.desc: The Set ID is the Template ID of the Template used.
